spinnova.origin: SPINNOVA is the fiber brand and technology of Spinnova Plc, a Finnish company. The feedstock is cellulose, principally wood pulp, and the producer states that the technology can also use waste streams such as textile, leather or agricultural residues. Commercial scaling has been uneven: Spinnova's joint venture with the pulp producer Suzano, Woodspin Oy, was placed on hold, and in 2025 Spinnova bought Suzano's stake in Woodspin and in Suzano Finland for a nominal two euros, ending the joint-venture arrangement.
spinnova.structure: SPINNOVA fiber is made of cellulose that has not been dissolved or regenerated. The producer describes the input as microfibrillated cellulose (MFC): pulp fibers mechanically broken down into a paste of fine cellulose fibrils. During spinning, these fibrils align with the flow and bond to one another by hydrogen bonding as the material dries, forming a fiber that is a network of native cellulose I fibrils rather than the cellulose II lattice found in viscose or lyocell. Public data on crystallinity, cross-section and dimensions are limited.
spinnova.process: Spinnova describes three main stages. First, pulp is mechanically refined into a fine microfibrillated cellulose suspension, without dissolving chemicals. Second, the suspension is pumped through a proprietary nozzle in which the fibrils rotate and orient along the flow, forming a continuous fiber. Third, the fiber is dried, with water evaporated rather than exchanged in a coagulation bath, and cut to staple for blending and spinning into yarn. The company states that the process creates no side streams and cites large water and CO2 reductions versus cotton; these are producer claims.
spinnova.performance: Detailed independent performance data remain scarce. The producer presents SPINNOVA as a cotton-like staple fiber that is normally blended with other fibers in yarns, which means the finished fabric's strength, moisture behavior and durability reflect the blend. As native cellulose, it is hydrophilic, chars rather than melts, and in principle accepts cellulose dye classes (reactive, direct, vat). Buyers should request test reports on the actual yarn, since strength of hydrogen-bonded fibril networks can differ markedly when wet.
spinnova.identify: Burn behavior should resemble other cellulose (paper-like odor, soft ash), but burn tests are indicative only. FTIR will identify cellulose, and X-ray diffraction could in principle distinguish its cellulose I structure from regenerated cellulose II, but no standard public method identifies the brand. Verification relies on supply-chain documents and the producer. The existing atlas base 'paper yarn' is an approximation: the fiber is not a cut paper strip.
spinnova.labeling: SPINNOVA is a trademark, not a generic fiber name. How this mechanically formed cellulose fiber should be named under the FTC generic-name rules (16 CFR 303.7) and the EU fiber-name list in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 could not be confirmed from public sources for this entry. Buyers should follow the producer's current labeling guidance, check the finished label, and treat environmental comparisons as producer claims.
spinnova.past: Spinnova was developed in Finland around the idea of forming textile fiber from cellulose mechanically rather than by dissolution. It then formed the Woodspin joint venture with the pulp producer Suzano to scale up production. In 2025, after a strategic review, Woodspin's operations were put on hold, Spinnova recognized an impairment of about 18.4 million euros on its Woodspin holding, withdrew financial guidance for 2025 and 2026, and acquired Suzano's stake for two euros, regaining the right to license its technology without restriction. Trade press later reported a textile-recycling consortium involving Spinnova and Circulose.
facts: Mechanical refining to microfibrillated cellulose, nozzle alignment, drying

infinna.origin: Infinna is the fiber brand of Infinited Fiber Company, a Finnish technology company. Its feedstock is cellulose-rich textile waste, mainly cotton-rich post-consumer textiles, and the fiber is a regenerated cellulose made via cellulose carbamate. The company has planned a first commercial factory of about 30,000 tonnes per year at Stora Enso's former Veitsiluoto paper-mill site in Kemi, Finland, an investment of around 400 million euros. As of a March 2026 report it had an environmental permit but no final investment decision.
infinna.structure: The finished fiber is regenerated cellulose. The key intermediate is cellulose carbamate, a cellulose derivative in which some hydroxyl groups carry carbamate (O-CO-NH2) groups formed by reaction with urea. The carbamate groups make the cellulose soluble in dilute alkali; after spinning, the regenerated fiber is essentially cellulose with a low residual carbamate content. The producer describes a cotton-like appearance, and its FAQ states claims such as good dye uptake. Independent structural data on crystallinity and cross-section are limited.
infinna.process: Infinited Fiber describes the route this way: textile waste is collected, sorted and shredded; non-cellulosic fibers such as polyester and elastane, dyes and finishes are removed; the recovered cellulose is activated and reacted with urea to form cellulose carbamate; the carbamate is dissolved in alkali to form a spinning solution; the solution is wet-spun into a coagulation bath, and the filaments are washed, dried and cut to staple. The approach adapts older carbamate research as an alternative to carbon disulfide-based viscose chemistry.
infinna.performance: Publicly available independent test data remain limited. As a regenerated cellulose it should absorb water readily, char rather than melt, and dye with reactive, direct and vat dyes. Infinited Fiber claims the fiber has a natural cotton-like look, good dye uptake and some antimicrobial properties, and that it is biodegradable and free of microplastics; these are producer statements whose test conditions should be requested. Strength and abrasion performance in finished fabrics depend on blend and yarn construction.
infinna.identify: Burn tests (indicative only) should show cellulose behavior: rapid burning, paper-like odor, little ash. FTIR identifies cellulose; residual carbamate nitrogen may be detectable by elemental analysis, but no standard public method identifies the brand. The atlas links Infinna to viscose as the nearest generic family, but the fiber is not made by the viscose process, so product labels may use a different name. Check the actual label and producer guidance.
infinna.labeling: Infinna is a trademark, not a generic name. Under the FTC rules (16 CFR 303.7) rayon covers regenerated cellulose, and the EU list in Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 distinguishes viscose, modal, lyocell and cupro by process; which name a carbamate fiber should carry could not be confirmed for this entry. Buyers should follow the producer's labeling guidance and verify recycled-content claims through documentation for the specific lot.
infinna.past: Infinited Fiber grew out of Finnish research on cellulose carbamate, a chemistry studied for decades as a viscose alternative, and set out to apply it to textile waste. In 2022 it chose Kemi for a first commercial factory. Trade press has reported funding of about 40 million euros backed in part by the parent companies of Zara, Uniqlo and H&M. Delivery dates have shifted, and by March 2026 the Kemi project had its environmental permit while the investment decision was still pending.
facts: Kemi, Finland, about 30,000 tonnes per year
environmental permit granted; no final investment decision
